title: Complexity of tolerant monotonicity testing
formal: Determine, up to multiplicative constants for each fixed pair \(0<a<b<1\), the asymptotic randomized adaptive query complexity \(Q(n;a,b)\) of distinguishing Boolean functions on \(\{0,1\}^n\) at uniform Hamming distance at most \(a\) from monotonicity from those at distance at least \(b\). The nonadaptive complexity is a distinct comparison problem and is not silently identified with \(Q\).
definitions:
The domain \(\{0,1\}^n\) has the coordinatewise partial order: \(x\le y\) if \(x_i\le y_i\) for all \(i\). A function \(g:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) is monotone if \(g(x)\le g(y)\) whenever \(x\le y\). For arbitrary \(f\), define \[\operatorname{dist}(f,\mathrm{MON}_n)=\min_{g\in\mathrm{MON}_n}2^{-n}|\{x:f(x)\ne g(x)\}|.\] The input function is unknown and is accessed by exact value queries at chosen vertices. Query locations may depend on all previous answers and internal randomness. Arbitrary computation between queries is free.

A tester must accept every function of distance at most \(a\) with probability at least \(2/3\), and reject every function of distance at least \(b\) with probability at least \(2/3\). No guarantee is imposed for distances strictly between the thresholds. Both types of errors are allowed. \(Q(n;a,b)\) is the smallest worst-case number of queries of any randomized decision tree satisfying these guarantees for all input functions. Probability is only over that tree's internal randomness. Repeated queries count as queries, and there is no free labelled sampling oracle; uniformly chosen test points can of course be queried. An entire truth-table query budget of \(2^n\) always makes the quantity finite.

The requested asymptotics take \(n\to\infty\) with \(a,b\) fixed; upper and lower multiplicative constants may depend on these thresholds. Since either the constant-zero or constant-one function differs from \(f\) on at most half the domain, every distance is at most \(1/2\). Therefore \(Q(n;a,b)=0\) when \(b>1/2\); those formal parameter pairs are trivial. The substantive regime has \(b\le1/2\).

A nonadaptive tester chooses all queried points before receiving any answers. A lower bound restricted to such testers does not automatically apply to the adaptive trees defining this card. Ordinary monotonicity testing is the separate case where the acceptance threshold is zero; tolerance here requires accepting all functions within positive distance \(a\).
answer_criterion: Supply explicit asymptotically matching upper and lower bounds for \(Q(n;a,b)\), with complete Lean-checked proofs and constants permitted to depend only on the fixed thresholds. Zero-query regimes must be identified separately. A determination only for nonadaptive queries, only for ordinary testing, or only up to unmatched exponential powers is partial progress. The precision is multiplicative asymptotic equivalence, not the numerical absolute-error tolerance applied to a query-count function.
context:
Chen and collaborators prove mildly exponential lower bounds for nonadaptive tolerant monotonicity testers with constant separation between the thresholds. Their theorem concerns nonadaptive, two-sided testing; it does not give the same bound for unrestricted adaptive testers.

The imported candidate did not specify adaptivity. This card explicitly selects the general adaptive complexity, retaining nonadaptive results as context. Thresholds remain parameters rather than replacing the question by one arbitrarily chosen pair.
why: Tolerance changes monotonicity testing from detecting defects to estimating distance, exposing a large unexplained query gap.

import_provenance.original_title: The complexity of tolerant monotonicity testing
import_provenance.original_statement: Determine the query complexity of distinguishing Boolean functions on {0,1}^n that are ε₁-close to monotone from those ε₂-far, for fixed 0<ε₁<ε₂. Even nonadaptive testing has an exponential gap in the exponent between 2^{Ω(n^{1/4})} lower bounds and roughly 2^{Õ(√n)} upper bounds; the power of adaptivity is also unresolved.
